Star
STāR
n. (rendering Hebrew kōkhāb and Greek astēr, astron)
From Old English steorra, common Germanic, cognate with Latin stella and Greek astēr. Genesis dispatches the entire host of them in four words — “he made the stars also” — an almost dismissive clause appended to the fourth day, and again the polemic is deliberate: the bodies that ruled the destinies of men in Babylonian religion are an afterthought in Moses' account, made by the same hand that made the lamps and hung in the same firmament.

Biblical Definition

The stars are creatures of the fourth day, innumerable to men and individually known to God: “He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names” (Psa 147:4). That verse is the whole doctrine in miniature — what is beyond counting to us is a named roll to Him, and the psalm sets it immediately beside His healing of the broken in heart, so that the God of the galaxies and the God of the wounded are shewn to be one God with one attention. To Abraham the stars became the sign of the promise, when God brought him forth and bade him tell them if he were able, and said, So shall thy seed be — a promise counted to him for righteousness. The star is also messianic: Balaam prophesied a Star out of Jacob, and the wise men said, “we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him” (Mat 2:2), coming to the child rather than to the sky. The Lord Jesus takes the title to Himself at the close of the canon: “I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). Finally the stars are the figure of the saints' glory. They that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever (Dan 12:3); and since one star differeth from another star in glory, the resurrection glory of the saints is real, ordered, and not uniform.

Webster 1828 Definition

The innumerable lights of the fourth day, each named and numbered by God; the sign of the promise to Abraham, the emblem of Christ as the bright and morning star, and the figure of the saints shining in resurrection glory.

expand to see more

STAR, n. 1. Any of the luminous bodies which appear in the heavens, and are supposed to be suns, each with its own system. He made the stars also. Genesis 1.

2. In Scripture, the stars are used as the emblem of a multitude beyond numbering. Tell the stars, if thou be able to number them; so shall thy seed be. Genesis 15.

3. A figure of Christ. There shall come a Star out of Jacob. Numbers 24. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. Rev. 22.

4. A figure of ministers and of the saints. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches. Rev. 1. They that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever and ever. Dan. 12.

5. The reading of the stars for the foretelling of events, called astrology, is the vain art of the Chaldeans, which the prophet derides and the law forbids. Isa. 47; Deut. 18.

Key Scripture

Psalm 147:4 — "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names."

Matthew 2:2 — "Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him."

Daniel 12:3 — "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever."

Revelation 22:16 — "I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star."

Modern Corruption

Astrology — the reading of the stars for guidance and destiny — is the corruption Scripture names most often and mocks most sharply, and it survives undiminished as entertainment that is still consulted in earnest.

expand to see more

Isaiah's taunt against Babylon is the sharpest thing in Scripture on the subject: let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee; behold, they shall be as stubble, the fire shall burn them. The mockery is aimed at a professional class that governed an empire's decisions. Daniel's narrative makes the same point by demonstration — the Chaldean astrologers could not tell the king his dream, and God's servant could, because there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets. The law forbids the practice with the other divinations of the nations, and Deu 4:19 explains the reason: the host of heaven was divided unto all nations as a gift, not appointed as an oracle.

It is objected that nobody takes horoscopes seriously now, and the objection understates how far the practice has revived. The claim being made is a real one — that character and future are written in the stars at birth — and it is a rival doctrine of providence, assigning to creatures the government that belongs to the Creator, and to fate the place that belongs to a Father. The star of Bethlehem is the exact counter-example that is usually cited in defence of the art: it did not disclose the future to the wise men, and it was not read by their skill; God moved a light to bring worshippers to His Son. The sign served the Word and led men to Christ, which is the opposite of what astrology does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kōkhāb covers every star and constellation, and is the word of Abraham's promise and Balaam's prophecy. Greek distinguishes astēr, the single star, from astron, the constellation or star-group.

expand to see more

Hebrew kōkhāb (H3556) — star; some 37 occurrences, including the Star out of Jacob (Num 24:17) and the morning stars singing together (Job 38:7).

Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — host; in the phrase the host of heaven, the stars considered as an ordered army, whence the divine title LORD of hosts.

Hebrew mazzālōth (H4208) — the twelve signs, the constellations of the zodiac; named in 2Ki 23:5 among the idolatries Josiah put down.

Greek astēr (G792) — a star; the word of the star in the east (Mat 2:2) and of the seven stars in the Lord's right hand (Rev 1:16).

Greek phōsphōros (G5459) — the light-bringer, the day star; used in 2Pe 1:19 of the day star arising in the heart, joined to the more sure word of prophecy.

Usage

"Of the created host: he made the stars also (Gen 1:16); he telleth the number of the stars (Psa 147:4); the host of heaven cannot be numbered (Jer 33:22)."

"Of the promise and the Messiah: so shall thy seed be (Gen 15:5); a Star out of Jacob (Num 24:17); we have seen his star in the east (Mat 2:2)."

"Of ministers and saints: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches (Rev 1:20); shining as the stars for ever and ever (Dan 12:3); one star differeth from another star in glory (1Co 15:41)."
